item.title: Reflecting On Failure(Unit 3)
item.description:
Learning To Reflect On Failure

Failure should be our teacher, not our undertaker. Failure is delay, not defeat. It is a temporary detour, not a dead end. Failure is something we can avoid only by saying nothing, doing nothing, and being nothing. ~ Denis Waitley

In Unit 3, I learned a lot more than I expected. Failure is not about acknowledging a mistake but understanding why we make a mistake and think about how we handle the situation. I recently had focused on the book “The Right Kind Of Wrong” By Amy Edmondson. My group, Group 1, was given the opportunity to read the Introduction for the book and summarize it for the class. I faced problems in covering the chapter due to its lengthy page count and the need to summarize the entire chapter in a few days. This combined with course work from other disciplines made it quite time-consuming. After summarizing and discussing with the group, I sat down and wrote the reflections I had for that chapter.

item.title: Learning Transformation And Composition(Unit2)
item.description:
Mixing Math and Pixels

After finishing Unit 1, we started off by learning about Image Transformations and its types. It was quite fun and interesting to learn about the different ways we can view and transform images in our computers. It also introduced us to the concepts of Functions. In math, I always thought functions were just dry equations in a textbook or problem. But as we started to learn about how images transform and how functions are involved in it, it became more than just another mathematics symbol. It started to look like a machine that takes a pixel and transforms it into something new. And when we start chaining those machines together, we get a composite. It gives us the ability to rotate, resize and blur images in one command rather than take 3 different steps.

item.title: The Way I See Information (Unit 1)
item.description:
The Change In Perspective

Before the start of my second semester, I did not know what I would learn in the course “Becoming A Reflective Information Scientist”. I guessed it would be somewhere on the lines of sociology and philosophy, mostly because we were doing similar courses in college even when our actual domains were in the field of sciences. Looking back at it, the course title was quite self-explanatory. To become a good information scientist one must not only know how to decipher information themselves but also have the ability to show that information in its most accurate and digestible form. We must be reflective individuals who can understand the data to its most basic forms and then show that information to the world. As Albert Einstein once said:
